patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Iain Wares: Edinburgh → South Africa; Birmingham → California: Fr James Robinson; Scotland → Toronto: Fr Paul Moore; Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander; England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa').
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Jimmy Savile: first report 1958, first action 2012 (54 years). Two police investigations in his lifetime (earliest 1958) produced no charges; Surrey Police 2007-09 dropped; BBC Newsnight report shelved Dec 2011; press inquiries from 1973 never published Cyril Smith MP: first report 1968, first action 2012 (44 years). A pupil told police in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; investigations in 1970, 1998, 1999 brought no charge; CPS said in 2012 he should have been charged over 40 years earlier Rotherham grooming networks: first report 1999, first action 2010 (11 years). Children's-home managers and Risky Business youth workers reported from the early-to-mid 1990s; researcher Angie Heal warned officials 2002-2007; a rape reported in 2001 led to release without charge Rochdale grooming ring: first report 2008, first action 2012 (4 years). A victim went to police in 2008 but the CPS declined to prosecute citing her credibility; NHS worker Sara Rowbotham's alerts were ignored; GMP apologised in 2015 for 2008-2010 failures Barry Bennell (English football): first report 1989, first action 1994 (5 years). A parent's anonymous letter to Crewe manager Dario Gradi (1989-90) asked for an investigation; the club kept him on with restrictions Kincora Boys' Home: first report 1977, first action 1980 (3 years). Allegations reached the RUC in 1977 and a report went to the DPP naming prominent businessmen, but no prosecution followed until press exposure; claims of M
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Scotland 2017: Limitation (Childhood Abuse) (Scotland) Act 2017 removed the three-year time bar for childhood abuse civil claims (announced in force 4 Oct 2017) England and Wales 2026: Crime and Policing Act 2026 s.96 removed the three-year limitation period for child sexual abuse personal-injury claims, retrospectively; in force 29 June 2026; defendants must show a fair trial is impossible
patterns.pattern_summary: Most people abused as children do not tell anyone for many years. In many countries and US states the legal deadline for suing or prosecuting, called a statute of limitations, used to run out in a person's early twenties, before most had spoken. When legislatures proposed extending these deadlines or reopening old claims, the institutions that would face lawsuits lobbied against the changes. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million on lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018. In Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference spent more than $7.6 million and the state's insurance federation nearly $20.7 million on lobbying from 2014 to 2024. These totals cover all the issues they lobbied on, not only this one. Where the deadlines were lifted anyway, many institutions filed for bankruptcy. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and religious orders did so, several of them hours or days before a trial, a deposition or a new law took effect. The Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics also filed.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2014: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), England and Wales; announced 7 July 2014, statutory from Feb 2015, final report 20 Oct 2022. 19 reports; Catholic Church report (Nov 2020) found it put reputation before children; first final recommendation fully implemented only in June 2026 (limitation reform)
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Holy See and IICSA (England & Wales): —
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into United Kingdom on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA. United Kingdom — forced adoption of unmarried mothers' babies 1949–1976 (JCHR 2022; apology 2026).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2003: Sexual Offences Act 2003 allows prosecution in England, Wales and NI of offences against children abroad (Scotland: 1995 Act); used to convict Richard Huckle in 2016 2019: Europol IOCTA 2019: live distant child abuse (LDCA) is the most common form of commercial child sexual exploitation; the Philippines remains the most prominent victim location; some offenders also travel; EU police urged to use PNR travel data
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role_note: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity (investigated and disproved). Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims (investigated and disproved). Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims (investigated and disproved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role_note: United Kingdom → Philippines demand for livestreamed abuse.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: United Kingdom — forced adoption of unmarried mothers' babies 1949–1976 (JCHR 2022; apology 2026); North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care'; Kincora Boys' Home, Belfast — Hart Inquiry findings; Lambeth Council children's homes (Shirley Oaks, South Vale, Angell Road) — IICSA; Nottinghamshire and Nottingham councils (incl. Beechwood) — IICSA; Medomsley Detention Centre, County Durham — Neville Husband and staff; Islington Council children's homes, London; Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse — final report (England and Wales); British child migration programmes — IICSA; Jimmy Savile — 'Giving Victims a Voice' (Met Police/NSPCC); Lampard report — Savile in NHS hospitals; Cyril Smith MP — Cambridge House and Knowl View, Rochdale; IICSA Westminster report — deference and failures (no proven 'VIP ring'); Lord Greville Janner — allegations from Leicestershire chil.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: False alarms that drown real cases
patterns.role_note: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity. Elm Guest House, London — VIP-abuse claims. Operation Midland — Carl Beech's false 'VIP ring' claims.
patterns.pattern_summary: False stories about child trafficking take police time and public attention away from real cases. In July 2020 a claim spread online that the furniture company Wayfair was selling children through its listings. The US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about it within days, and Polaris, the charity that runs the hotline, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed help; none of the reports contained new information. In 2016 a false claim known as "Pizzagate", that a Washington pizza restaurant was the centre of a child-abuse ring, led a man to fire a rifle inside the restaurant. In London, the Metropolitan Police spent more than £2 million on Operation Midland, which investigated claims made by Carl Beech about a ring of powerful men; the claims were false, Beech was jailed for perverting the course of justice, and he had separately admitted child sexual offences. In the 1980s the McMartin preschool case in California, built on claims of ritual abuse, cost about $14 million and ended without a conviction.

cases.title: North Wales children's homes — Waterhouse Inquiry 'Lost in Care'
cases.who: Clwyd and Gwynedd county councils' children's homes, incl. Bryn Estyn; North Wales Police criticised
cases.what: Sir Ronald Waterhouse's tribunal took evidence from about 650 people who had been in care and published 'Lost in Care' in February 2000, finding widespread abuse over about 20 years in children's homes in North Wales. Allegations were reported across almost 40 homes, with the report concentrating on seven. Seven former care workers were convicted after a 1991 police inquiry, five of them from Bryn Estyn. The report found responses were 'too little and too late' and that children's interests were sacrificed to protect professional positions; officers of North Wales Police were among those accused.
cases.cover_up: The earlier Jillings report (commissioned 1994, completed 1996) was shelved and only released in redacted form in 2012 after a BBC Freedom of Information request. North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers rather than having them independently investigated.

cases.title: Kincora Boys' Home, Belfast — Hart Inquiry findings
cases.who: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast Welfare Authority / Eastern Health and Social Services Board); RUC investigations; MI5
cases.what: The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry chaired by Sir Anthony Hart reported on 20 January 2017. It confirmed that 38 boys at Kincora were sexually abused; three staff members, Joseph Mains, Raymond Semple and William McGrath, were convicted. Hart found that Kincora was not a homosexual brothel, that no security agency used it to entrap or blackmail men, and that there was 'no credible evidence' that prominent people such as civil servants, businessmen or Sir Maurice Oldfield were involved; he called the honey-trap claims 'unfounded myths'. He did criticise MI5 for obstructing the 1980s police investigation. Some former residents rejected the conclusions.
cases.cover_up: Hart found MI5 'consistently obstructed a proper line of inquiry' during the 1980s RUC Caskey Phase Three investigation, and found numerous missed opportunities to detect and stop the abuse.

cases.title: Lambeth Council children's homes (Shirley Oaks, South Vale, Angell Road) — IICSA
cases.who: London Borough of Lambeth; Shirley Oaks, South Vale and Angell Road children's homes
cases.what: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse reported on 27 July 2021 that children in Lambeth's care were subjected to decades of cruelty and sexual abuse from the 1960s. By June 2020 the council had complaints from 705 former residents; at Shirley Oaks, allegations were made against 177 staff or associated people involving at least 529 former residents. At Angell Road, children including some under five were systematically exposed to sexual abuse. The inquiry found racism, nepotism, corruption and mismanagement in the council, and that most children at Shirley Oaks (1980) and South Vale (1990–91) were Black.
cases.cover_up: Over 40 years only one senior employee was disciplined. The council did not tell a coroner that a boy found dead at Shirley Oaks in 1977 had alleged sexual abuse by his 'house father' Donald Hosegood; the inquiry asked the Metropolitan Police to consider a criminal investigation into this.

cases.title: Nottinghamshire and Nottingham councils (incl. Beechwood) — IICSA
cases.who: Nottinghamshire County Council and Nottingham City Council residential and foster care; Beechwood Children's Home
cases.what: IICSA reported on 31 July 2019 that sexual abuse was widespread in the two councils' residential and foster care in the 1970s–1990s. About 350 people reported abuse. From the late 1970s to 2019, 16 residential staff and 10 foster carers were convicted of sexually abusing children in their care, plus 12 convictions for harmful sexual behaviour by children against other children. The inquiry concluded that 'neither of the Councils learned from their mistakes'.
cases.cover_up: Only two disciplinary actions, both inadequate, followed the many allegations at Beechwood; known perpetrators were allowed to continue fostering and abused again.

cases.title: Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse — final report (England and Wales)
cases.who: Institutions across England and Wales: local authority care, churches, schools, custodial institutions, political parties, police
cases.what: IICSA published its final report in October 2022 after 19 investigation reports, 325 days of public hearings, more than 700 live witnesses and almost 1,000 written statements, and over 200,000 documents. More than 6,200 victims and survivors took part in its Truth Project. It made 107 recommendations, including mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse. Its investigations found institutional failures by councils, police, churches and government departments.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Jimmy Savile — 'Giving Victims a Voice' (Met Police/NSPCC)
cases.who: Jimmy Savile (BBC broadcaster); BBC; NHS hospitals; Metropolitan Police
cases.what: After Savile's death in October 2011, an ITV documentary, 'Exposure: The Other Side of Jimmy Savile', broadcast on 3 Oct 2012, carried accounts of abuse of under-age teenage girls. The Metropolitan Police opened a criminal investigation, Operation Yewtree, on 19 Oct 2012. The January 2013 Met/NSPCC report 'Giving Victims a Voice' recorded 214 crimes across 28 police force areas, including 34 rape or penetration offences, from 1955 to 2009; 450 people had made allegations against him, 73% of them under 18 at the time. The CPS apologised for missing the chance to prosecute him in 2009. The report found no clear evidence that he operated in a paedophile ring.
cases.cover_up: Earliest known police report dates from 1958, with police intelligence from 1963; Surrey Police investigated in 2007–09 without charges. A BBC Newsnight investigation was shelved in December 2011; the Pollard Review called the decision flawed.
cases.network: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)

cases.title: Lampard report — Savile in NHS hospitals
cases.who: NHS hospitals (Leeds General Infirmary, Stoke Mandeville, Broadmoor and others)
cases.what: Kate Lampard's lessons-learned report (26 February 2015) drew on 44 NHS investigation reports — 28 published in June 2014 and 16 more alongside her report — and found Savile's known victims in NHS hospitals were aged five to 75, including patients, staff and visitors; his status gave him keys and virtually unfettered access to wards. At Leeds General Infirmary 64 people came forward and 60 alleged abuse on the premises, between 1962 and 2009, including three rapes.
cases.network: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)

cases.title: Cyril Smith MP — Cambridge House and Knowl View, Rochdale
cases.who: Cyril Smith (Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992); Lancashire Constabulary; Director of Public Prosecutions; Rochdale Council
cases.what: Cyril Smith, Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992, was alleged by eight men to have indecently assaulted them as teenagers in about 1961–1966; six had lived at Cambridge House hostel, which he helped set up. The Director of Public Prosecutions advised against prosecution in 1970, and CPS reviews in 1998 and 1999 did not lead to charges. He died on 3 September 2010, never charged. On 27 November 2012 Greater Manchester Police said the boys had been victims of physical and sexual abuse by Smith, and the CPS said he should have been charged. The IICSA report on Cambridge House, Knowl View and Rochdale (April 2018) found no evidence of improper influence on the DPP but said valuable opportunities to prosecute were lost in 1998 and 1999, and that discussions before his 1988 knighthood showed 'considerable deference to power'; witnesses also told it Smith assaulted boys at Knowl View School.
cases.cover_up: Police evidence presented in 1970 led to no action; the CPS said in 2012 that Smith should have been charged and that he had been given an assurance in 1970 he would not be prosecuted. Press allegations in 1979 (Rochdale Alternative Press, Private Eye) produced no prosecution. He was knighted in 1988 though Margaret Thatcher had been told of the allegations.

cases.title: IICSA Westminster report — deference and failures (no proven 'VIP ring')
cases.who: Parliament; political parties; police; Director of Public Prosecutions
cases.what: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse examined how Parliament, political parties, the police, prosecutors and the honours system dealt with allegations of child sexual abuse involving people connected to Westminster, and reported on 25 February 2020. It found "no evidence to suggest an organised network of abusers in Westminster". It did find "overt and direct deference by police towards powerful people", that the diplomat Sir Peter Hayman "was the beneficiary of preferential, differential and unduly deferential treatment", that party whips' offices were "concerned above all to protect the image of their party" though there was no evidence they deliberately suppressed specific information, that the former Liberal leader David Steel "yielded to considerations of political expediency" over Cyril Smith, and that the honours system in some instances "prioritised reputation and discretion with little or no regard for victims".
cases.cover_up: The inquiry concluded that "deference to class and power was the overriding motive" for decisions in the Montagu and Hayman cases, and that the police showed "a patronising attitude" towards a working-class victim in the Montagu case.

cases.title: Lord Greville Janner — allegations from Leicestershire children's homes; never tried
cases.who: Greville Janner (Labour MP and peer); Leicestershire Police; Crown Prosecution Service
cases.what: Allegations that Janner abused boys in Leicestershire children's homes first emerged publicly in 1991. In April 2015 the CPS decided not to charge him because of dementia; an independent review reversed this in June 2015, but he was found unfit to stand trial in Dec 2015 and died on 19 Dec 2015 before a 'trial of the facts'. He was never convicted. A January 2016 report by retired judge Sir Richard Henriques found that the CPS and Leicestershire Police had mishandled investigations in 1991, 2002 and 2007 and that there had been enough evidence to prosecute him in 2007.
cases.cover_up: Police investigated in 1991, 2002 and 2007 without charges. The Henriques report (Jan 2016) found the CPS and police at fault and said a prosecution was likely to have succeeded in 1991, 2002 or 2007. A 2021 review found police 'appeared reluctant to fully investigate'.

cases.title: Rotherham — Jay inquiry (1,400 children, 1997–2013)
cases.who: Group-based exploitation networks; Rotherham Metropolitan Borough Council; South Yorkshire Police
cases.what: Professor Alexis Jay's independent inquiry, published 26 August 2014, estimated that about 1,400 children were sexually exploited in Rotherham between 1997 and 2013, some as young as 11. It described the collective failures of the council and South Yorkshire Police as 'blatant'. The report said most known perpetrators were of Pakistani heritage, and that frontline staff were confused about what might be seen as racist. The council leader resigned within hours of publication.
cases.cover_up: Three earlier reports (2002, 2003, 2013) on exploitation were effectively suppressed or ignored; police did not treat the abuse as a priority.

cases.title: Telford — Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Exploitation
cases.who: Group-based exploitation networks; West Mercia Police; Telford & Wrekin Council
cases.what: The inquiry chaired by Tom Crowther QC, published 12 July 2022, found more than 1,000 children were sexually exploited in Telford over at least 30 years. Agencies dismissed the abuse as 'child prostitution', blamed children for 'lifestyle choices', and failed to investigate partly from nervousness about race. Seven men were jailed in 2013 after Operation Chalice. West Mercia Police and the council apologised; the inquiry found no evidence of corruption.
cases.cover_up: Concerns raised by officers, youth workers and teachers in the 1990s were not taken seriously; specialist CSE teams were cut to near zero after Operation Chalice.

cases.title: Oldham — 2022 assurance review
cases.who: Oldham Council; Greater Manchester Police; shisha bars, residential homes and taxis
cases.what: The review published 20 June 2022 found 'serious failings' by Oldham Council and Greater Manchester Police: police and council knew of risks from shisha bars by late 2010 yet children of 13 and 14 still visited them in 2013, and multi-agency child-protection procedures were often not started. It criticised how a former council welfare rights officer, later convicted of rape and trafficking, was investigated. The review found no evidence of a cover-up by senior managers or councillors. Oldham is the first confirmed area for local investigation under the 2025 national inquiry.

cases.title: Casey national audit on group-based child sexual exploitation
cases.who: Home Office; police forces in England and Wales
cases.what: Baroness Casey's audit, published 16 June 2025, found that data flaws meant the scale of group-based exploitation could not be assessed, and that perpetrator ethnicity was not recorded for about two-thirds of cases. Local data from three police force areas showed 'disproportionate numbers of men from Asian ethnic backgrounds amongst suspects', which she said warranted further examination; she said flawed data had been used to dismiss concerns. The government accepted all 12 recommendations, including mandatory ethnicity and nationality data for suspects, charging adult sex with under-16s as rape, an NCA-led national operation, and a national inquiry with statutory powers.

cases.title: UK — IICSA finds gaps let known offenders abuse children abroad (2020)
cases.who: UK Home Office, police, courts
cases.what: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse report on the protection of children outside the UK (January 2020) found that only 11 of the 5,551 Sexual Harm Prevention Orders made in 2017/18 included foreign-travel restrictions, that 361 UK nationals sought consular help after arrest abroad for child sex offences in 2013–2017, and that there appear to have been only about eight successful UK prosecutions since 1997 for offences committed abroad, including Keith Morris (18.5 years, Kenya) and Mark Frost (Thailand).
cases.cover_up: IICSA found travel restrictions were rarely used: 11 of 5,551 Sexual Harm Prevention Orders in 2017/18 and six Sexual Risk Orders in force in March 2019.

flows.what: British child migration to Canada began in the 19th century; IICSA found the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to sexual abuse allegations at its schools in Canada.

flows.what: New Zealand's Social Development Minister said in November 2009 that 549 British child migrants arrived between 1948 and 1954 and that most were placed in foster care rather than institutions; IICSA lists New Zealand among the destinations of British child migration.

flows.title: UK → Southern Rhodesia child migrants (Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College)
flows.what: IICSA found that children who told the headmaster they had been sexually abused by a padre at the college were beaten and warned against 'spreading malicious lies'; it lacked evidence to say whether Fairbridge UK knew of the allegations.

flows.title: Gary Glitter: UK → Cambodia → Vietnam
flows.what: After his 1999 UK conviction, Paul Gadd moved to Cambodia (expelled 2002–03) and then Vietnam, where he was convicted in 2006 of obscene acts with girls aged 10 and 11.

flows.title: Iain Wares: Edinburgh → South Africa
flows.what: Fettes College dismissed teacher Iain Wares in 1979 but gave him a glowing testimonial; he went on to teach in South Africa, where he later abused children. South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, which he was still contesting in 2025.

flows.title: United Kingdom → Philippines demand for livestreamed abuse
flows.what: IJM UK states the UK is among the top three global consumers of livestreamed abuse of Filipino children.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in Bulgaria (IWF 2025)
flows.what: Bulgaria hosted 87,959 URLs actioned by IWF in 2025, up from 9% share in 2024, driven by 'just a few particular sites'.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in the United States (IWF 2025)
flows.what: US hosting services held 49,021 URLs actioned by IWF in 2025.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: Scouting organisations (national Scout associations)
networks.what: National Scout associations; the Boy Scouts of America faced more than 82,000 sexual abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy and had kept internal 'ineligible volunteer' files on suspected abusers.

networks.name: Jeffrey Epstein and associates
networks.what: Financier Jeffrey Epstein (d. 2019) and Ghislaine Maxwell (convicted 2021) sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005 across homes in New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, the US Virgin Islands, Paris and London. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel was charged in France and died in custody. Banks paid hundreds of millions in settlements. 2025–2026 file releases led to misconduct and corruption inquiries against officials in the UK and Norway.

networks.name: Jimmy Savile and the institutions that hosted him (BBC, NHS)
networks.what: Savile used his BBC celebrity and NHS fundraising roles to gain access to children and patients for decades. Inquiries found 72 victims linked to the BBC (Smith, 2016) and victims aged 5–75 across NHS sites (Lampard, 2015); the Met recorded 214 crimes (2013).

networks.name: Operation Yewtree (UK entertainment figures)
networks.what: Metropolitan Police investigation opened 19 Oct 2012 after the Savile revelations; 19 arrests and 7 convictions of entertainment figures.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2010: Deetman Commission (set up by the Church March 2010), report 16 Dec 2011. At least 800 priests, monks and religious involved in abuse 1945-1985 (105 alive); estimated 10,000-20,000 minors abused; policy of "not hanging out the dirty washing"
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. The research for this map found no national inquiry in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2021: suspension: Netherlands suspends all intercountry adoption with immediate effect after Joustra committee report (8 February) 2024: ban: Netherlands announces citizens will no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad (May)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2013: Terre des Hommes "Sweetie" sting: 20,000 internet users in 10 weeks offered to pay for webcam sex with an apparent Filipino child; of 21,000 perpetrators, 1,000 were identified (from Australia, Canada, Germany, India, the Netherlands, the UK, the US and others), incl. 110 in the UK and 254 in the US — early evidence of "webcam child sex tourism"
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 33,788 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (11% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended; De Winter Commission — violence in Dutch youth care since 1945.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: De Winter Commission — violence in Dutch youth care since 1945
cases.who: Dutch residential youth care, foster care, juvenile justice institutions, closed youth care, shelters for unaccompanied asylum-seeking minors, institutions for disabled children
cases.what: The commission led by Professor Micha de Winter published 'Onvoldoende beschermd' on 14 June 2019 after interviewing about 1,000 people who had lived in foster families or youth institutions. It found that a considerable share of children in Dutch youth care since 1945 were not adequately protected from physical, psychological and sexual violence, that supervisors did not intervene enough, and that the government did too little to prevent it. The cabinet said the violence 'should never have happened' and set up a payment scheme for victims.

cases.title: Operation Torpedo — FBI ran three Tor sites
cases.who: Three Tor-hidden abuse sites run by a Nebraska man
cases.what: Dutch police compromised one site and found it physically hosted at a Nebraska web host; the FBI found an employee running two sites at work and one at home. After a year of surveillance the FBI arrested him and operated the sites for two weeks, using a network investigative technique to reveal visitors' IP addresses. The US DOJ said in December 2015 that 18 US users had been convicted besides the operator; one was the acting cybersecurity director of the US Department of Health and Human Services.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law
cases.who: Greek state institutions and foundling homes; AHEPA and other US agencies and proxy-adoption intermediaries
cases.what: Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many called 'orphans' after the civil war or born 'illegitimate', were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures. A law published on 2 May 2025 recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to records. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s that has not been carried out.
cases.cover_up: The adoptions were covered by confidentiality and secrecy; many adoptees lacked papers proving their origins.

cases.title: Samson Commission — sexual abuse of children in Dutch state care
cases.who: Dutch children's homes and foster care (Jeugdzorg)
cases.what: The commission chaired by former procurator-general Rieke Samson reported in October 2012 on sexual abuse of children in state-arranged care since 1945. It received 800 claims, 65% about children's homes and 30% about foster families, and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor. It found the government, care homes and foster care services did not do enough to protect children and, once aware, lacked professionalism and courage to act.

cases.title: Netherlands — National Rapporteur estimate of exploited Dutch girls
cases.who: Domestic pimps and 'loverboy' recruiters
cases.what: A report by National Rapporteur Corinne Dettmeijer, prepared with UNODC and published 18 October 2017, estimated that at least 1,320 underage Dutch girls aged 12 to 17 fall victim to sexual exploitation in the Netherlands each year, using 2012–2016 data. Underage girls made up nearly half of female victims in the Dutch sex industry. In October 2025 the current rapporteur reported reported exploitation cases rising from 868 (2023) to 944 (2024), with more teenage victims.

cases.title: Deetman Commission — Catholic Church in the Netherlands
cases.who: Catholic dioceses and religious orders in the Netherlands
cases.what: The commission led by former minister Wim Deetman, set up by the church in March 2010, reported on 16 December 2011. It identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated tens of thousands of victims. It found bishops and officials knew of the abuse and followed a policy of avoiding scandal.
cases.cover_up: Policy of 'not hanging out the dirty washing'; bishops and officials knew and did not act

cases.title: Utrecht University / WODC study — Jehovah's Witnesses in the Netherlands
cases.who: Jehovah's Witnesses (Netherlands)
cases.what: A study by Utrecht University researchers led by Kees van den Bos, commissioned by the Ministry of Justice's research centre WODC, was published on 23 January 2020. 751 participants reported experiences; only 27% of cases led to a police report. Victims were critical of internal handling by elders; the researchers recommended better support, elder training, an internal reporting centre, and that lawmakers consider a duty to report abuse to police.
cases.network: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
cases.who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
cases.what: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

flows.title: Seoul → Netherlands
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Netherlands; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Colombo → Netherlands
flows.what: Sri Lankan babies adopted to the Netherlands in the 1980s, many through baby farms and falsified papers; others went to the UK, Sweden, Denmark and Germany.

flows.title: Athens → Netherlands
flows.what: Greek-born children adopted to Netherlands 1950–1975; Greece restored their citizenship by law on 2 May 2025.

flows.title: Buyers in 24 countries → Philippines (HSI data)
flows.what: Europol's 2024 sprint on US HSI data: chats between about 12,000 criminal customer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines; packages may lead 24 countries to 197 buyers. Origin point is The Hague (sprint host), not a buyer country.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in the Netherlands (IWF 2025)
flows.what: The Netherlands was the largest host of IWF-actioned material for years (47% in 2018); its share fell to 11% in 2025. INHOPE 2025 still ranks it first for confirmed CSAM (36%).

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Dreamboard
networks.what: Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Boystown
networks.what: Tor platform with 400,000 registered users; four German administrators sentenced 7–12 years (2022).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: The Com
networks.what: Transnational network of online groups (incl. 764, CVLT) involved in sextortion, child sexual exploitation, swatting and other crimes; FBI public warning 23 July 2025; Europol Project COMPASS since 2025. Start year approximate.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi; Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Lateran concordat and Italian reporting (2012): —
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No national inquiry into institutional abuse found
patterns.role_note: "There are no official statistics"; under the Lateran concordat the Italian Bishops' Conference said in May 2012 its priests have no obligation to report suspected abuse to police; victims group Rete l'Abuso has demanded an independent external inquiry for years
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Nigeria — cult-linked networks traffic women and girls to Europe and West African mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Nigerian organized trafficking networks, some linked to cult organizations/confraternities
cases.what: The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report says highly organized groups, sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations or confraternities, recruit and exploit Nigerian women and girls in sex trafficking in Italy, Spain and the UK, and that networks move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. In the reporting year courts convicted 49 traffickers and the government identified 2,058 victims. It describes corruption and official complicity, including among officials responsible for anti-trafficking, as significant concerns.

cases.title: Romania — girls in state institutions at risk; victims sent across Europe (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers; staff of some government-run institutions
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says most identified victims are women and girls exploited in Romania and in Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK; children in government-run institutions, particularly girls in homes for persons with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking; and Roma children as young as 11 are 'sold' into marriage. Courts convicted 161 traffickers (143 for sex trafficking) and 600 victims were identified in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Alleged complicity, misconduct and negligence by government employees in cases involving children in government-run homes remained a concern.

cases.title: Bibbiano ('Angeli e Demoni') — investigation into unlawful removal of children
cases.who: Val d'Enza social services; mayor Andrea Carletti (house arrest 2019)
cases.what: In June 2019 Reggio Emilia prosecutors announced the 'Angeli e Demoni' investigation into Val d'Enza social services, alleging that children were wrongly removed from their families and placed in foster care on the basis of falsified reports; Bibbiano's mayor Andrea Carletti was placed under house arrest (confirmed in August 2019). Psychotherapist Claudio Foti was convicted at a fast-track trial but acquitted on appeal, and Italy's Court of Cassation confirmed his acquittal in June 2023. Carletti was acquitted in October 2024. On 9 July 2025 the Reggio Emilia court acquitted 11 of the remaining 14 defendants, many because 'the fact does not exist', and gave three light suspended sentences, the longest two years for the former head of social services. The case fits the 'adoption' setting more naturally.

cases.title: Hugh Nelson — first UK prosecution for AI-made abuse images
cases.who: Individual offender selling commissioned AI-transformed images
cases.what: Nelson, 27, used 3D software with an AI function to turn ordinary photos of real children, some supplied by people who knew them, into abuse imagery, selling it in chatrooms for about £5,000 over 18 months. Greater Manchester Police caught him after he told an undercover officer he charged £80 per 'character'. Convicted of 16 offences including encouraging the rape of a child under 13, he was sentenced at Bolton Crown Court on 28 October 2024 to 18 years. Police identified suspects and victims in Italy, France and the US.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Black Axe in Palermo — 14 convicted (2018), 4 acquitted of mafia association (2019)
cases.who: Black Axe (Nigerian confraternity) cell in Palermo
cases.what: A Palermo police operation on 18 November 2016 arrested 19 alleged members of a Black Axe cell based in the Ballarò district; prosecutors said it ran debt collection, exploitation of prostitution and drug trafficking with mafia-style initiation rites. On 21 May 2018 a Palermo judge (fast-track procedure) convicted 14 Nigerians to a combined 87 years. In November 2019 the Palermo Corte d'Assise, trying five others, did not accept the mafia-association charge: four were acquitted and one was jailed for 11 years for kidnapping and sexual violence.
cases.network: Black Axe (Neo-Black Movement of Africa confraternity)

cases.title: Próvolo Institute, Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza) — convictions 2019
cases.who: Provolo Institute for the Deaf (Argentina branch); Fr Nicola Corradi, Fr Horacio Corbacho, gardener Armando Gómez; Sr Kumiko Kosaka charged
cases.what: Priests Nicola Corradi (Italian) and Horacio Corbacho and other staff of the Provolo school for deaf children in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza were arrested in 2016, charged with abusing at least two dozen students. On 25 November 2019 a Mendoza court convicted Corradi, Corbacho and gardener Armando Gómez of abusing children at the school between 2004 and 2016; the victims in the trial were 10 former students. Corradi was sentenced to 42 years, Corbacho to 45 and Gómez to 18. Nun Kumiko Kosaka was charged in 2017 with helping the abuse and with physically abusing students.
cases.cover_up: Corradi had been accused in Verona in 2009 yet continued at the Argentine school; Japanese nun Kumiko Kosaka charged with abuse and covering up

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
cases.who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
cases.what: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
cases.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
cases.what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

cases.title: Operation Atlantic — FBI and EU follow-up to Boylover network
cases.who: Online offender networks incl. members of the Boylover network
cases.what: A joint FBI–EU investigation coordinated by Europol from November 2010. By February 2012, 37 child sex offenders had been identified and 17 arrested for molestation and production of illegal content; 8 victims were identified. Two targets had been members of the Boylover network tackled in Operation Rescue.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Chemosh — minors sharing abuse 'stickers' in WhatsApp groups
cases.who: Encrypted chat groups, many members minors
cases.what: Begun in 2017 after a public report about children forming WhatsApp groups to create and exchange abuse material, including emoji 'stickers'. Thirty-three investigations were opened (26 in Spain) with arrests in Spain, Italy and France; the average age of those arrested in Spain was 22 because many were minors.

flows.title: Seoul → Italy
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Italy; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Bucharest → Italy
flows.what: Romanian intercountry adoptions to Italy in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.

flows.title: Edo State → Libya → Italy (sex trafficking of women and girls)
flows.what: Women and girls, most from Edo State, are moved overland through Niger and Libya and by boat to Italy, bound by debt and oaths. IOM recorded an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims arriving by sea in 2014–2017.

flows.title: Italy / Germany / Switzerland → Kenya coast (tourist offenders)
flows.what: The 2006 UNICEF–Government study found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of clients of exploited children on the coast; Kenyans were 38 per cent.

flows.title: Phoenix → Rome: Joseph Henn (fugitive 2003–2019)
flows.what: Indicted in Arizona in 2003, the Salvatorian priest went to Italy and evaded a confirmed extradition until his arrest in Rome in May 2019.

flows.title: Verona → Mendoza: Fr Nicola Corradi
flows.what: Corradi, accused at the Provolo deaf school in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, worked at the order's school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and in 2019 sentenced to 42 years for abusing deaf children.

networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).
