networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Black Axe (Neo-Black Movement of Africa confraternity)
networks.what: Nigerian confraternity whose members in Italy were arrested in 2016 for 'mafia conspiracy, drug trafficking, exploitation of prostitution and violent crimes'. A Palermo court convicted 14 in 2018; in 2019 another Palermo court rejected the mafia-association charge for five others.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Legion of Christ (Legionaries of Christ)
networks.what: Founded in Mexico in 1941 by Marcial Maciel. The Vatican said in 2010 that Maciel committed 'true crimes' and the Legion had shielded him, and placed it under a papal delegate. The Legion's December 2019 report acknowledged 175 minors abused 1941–2019, 60 by Maciel and the rest by 33 priests.

networks.name: Congregation of Christian Brothers
networks.what: Irish-founded teaching order. The Ryan Report found sexual abuse 'endemic' in its Irish industrial schools; 11 Brothers were convicted over Mount Cashel in Canada; Australia's Royal Commission found 22% of Brothers were alleged perpetrators since 1950. Its North American province filed for bankruptcy in 2011 and paid US$16.5 million to 400 victims.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2025: report: Swedish state inquiry report on intercountry adoption (2 June 2025)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 6,820 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (2% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law
cases.who: Greek state institutions and foundling homes; AHEPA and other US agencies and proxy-adoption intermediaries
cases.what: Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many called 'orphans' after the civil war or born 'illegitimate', were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures. A law published on 2 May 2025 recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to records. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s that has not been carried out.
cases.cover_up: The adoptions were covered by confidentiality and secrecy; many adoptees lacked papers proving their origins.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Operation Atelier — network of abuse photographers
cases.who: Professional photographers producing abuse material
cases.what: Czech-initiated and supported by Europol and Eurojust: a Czech photographer exploited socially and financially disadvantaged children (close to 70) and, with a Swedish partner, distributed images to customers in the EU and Canada. In 2014 ten people were arrested in the Czech Republic (5), Sweden (2), France, Ireland and Spain; 30 TB of data were seized.

patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial) (receiving or involved). Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova. Ukraine — Ukrainian children given Russian citizenship and adopted into Russian families.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.
cases.network: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Ukraine — Ukrainian children given Russian citizenship and adopted into Russian families
cases.who: Russian state; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 30 May 2022 President Putin signed a decree easing Russian citizenship for Ukrainian children so they could be adopted by Russian families; Russia created a register of families wishing to adopt Ukrainian children and paid families per adopted child granted citizenship. Lvova-Belova said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. On 17 March 2023 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL (14 February 2023) documented a 'systematic' programme of re-education and adoption. (Deportations and camps are recorded by the conflict agent; this record covers the adoption element.)

cases.title: Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova
cases.who: Russian state: President Vladimir Putin; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 17 March 2023 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia, committed from at least 24 February 2022. The UN Commission of Inquiry found a transfer of 31 children in May 2022 was unlawful deportation and a war crime; Lvova-Belova's own bulletin said 380 orphans had been placed with Russian foster families and about 2,000 children from institutions transferred in February 2022. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for 're-education'.

cases.title: Ukraine orphanages as a 'recruitment tool' for traffickers — Disability Rights International 'No Way Home'
cases.who: Ukrainian state orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities
cases.what: Disability Rights International investigated 33 institutions between 2012 and 2015 and published 'No Way Home' in 2015. La Strada Ukraine told DRI that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme' and that sexual exploitation in institutions typically begins around age 13, often instigated by staff; an IOM counter-trafficking coordinator called orphanages a direct feeder to domestic and international trafficking and said most documented cases originate in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. DRI concluded that the orphanage system serves as a recruitment tool for traffickers.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Ukraine — wartime risk to evacuated institutional children; officials allegedly complicit (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Criminal networks; some institution officials
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says child sex trafficking in Ukraine is underreported and criminals are trying to build online networks to exploit Ukrainian children internationally; children evacuated from at least 195 facilities, including those with disabilities, are at high risk; and Ukrainian refugee women and children are vulnerable in Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Bulgaria and the UK. Ukraine convicted 24 traffickers in 2024, only six with prison terms.
cases.cover_up: Officials of several state-run residential institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent in trafficking of children in their care; no complicit officials convicted for the eighth year running.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Canada → Rome: Fr Bernard Prince; Orán → Vatican: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta; Dominican Republic → Vatican: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

cases.title: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child — Holy See review (2014)
cases.who: Holy See
cases.what: On 5 February 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said it was gravely concerned that the Holy See had not acknowledged the extent of the crimes, had not taken the necessary measures against child sexual abuse, and had adopted policies that allowed abuse to continue. It said the Holy See had consistently placed the church's reputation and the protection of perpetrators above children's best interests, accused it of transferring abusive priests to new parishes, urged it to require clergy to report abuse to police, and criticised a 'code of silence' under which whistleblowers were ostracised, demoted and fired.
cases.cover_up: Committee found abusive clergy were reassigned without police notification, bishops not required to report to civil authorities, and a code of silence

cases.title: McCarrick Report (Holy See, November 2020)
cases.who: Holy See; former Cardinal Theodore McCarrick
cases.what: The Holy See's report of 10 November 2020 found that Pope John Paul II appointed Theodore McCarrick Archbishop of Washington in 2000 despite a letter from Cardinal John O'Connor dated 28 October 1999 warning that the appointment would risk serious scandal, and after McCarrick denied the allegations. Benedict XVI did not order an investigation but had McCarrick told to retire in 2006 and keep a lower profile, which he did not do. The report said Francis did not learn that McCarrick was accused of abusing a minor until 2017. On 11 January 2019 the CDF found him guilty of solicitation in confession and sexual offences with minors and adults, and he was dismissed from the priesthood (announced 16 February 2019). A Massachusetts charge of assaulting a 16-year-old at a 1974 wedding reception was dismissed on 30 August 2023 after he was found incompetent to stand trial because of dementia. He died in April 2025.
cases.cover_up: A 1999 warning letter reached Pope John Paul II; an inquiry stalled after three of four US bishops gave 'inaccurate and incomplete information'; McCarrick was promoted to Washington in 2000

cases.title: Vatican tribunal — diplomat Carlo Capella and the Martinelli trial
cases.who: Holy See diplomat Mgr Carlo Capella; St Pius X pre-seminary
cases.what: On 23 June 2018 the Vatican tribunal convicted Mgr Carlo Capella, recalled in 2017 from the Holy See's embassy in Washington, of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years. In October 2020 the first Vatican criminal trial for sexual abuse began: Fr Gabriele Martinelli was accused of abusing an altar boy at the St Pius X pre-seminary inside the Vatican, and former rector Enrico Radice was charged with aiding and abetting.

cases.title: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta of Orán — convicted 2022
cases.who: Diocese of Orán; Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta
cases.what: Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from the Diocese of Orán in August 2017, citing health, after complaints from clergy, and in December 2017 Pope Francis gave him a post created for him at the Vatican's patrimony office (APSA). Clergy had complained to the nunciature in 2015–2016 about his behaviour with seminarians and explicit images on his phone. On 4 March 2022 a court in Salta sentenced him to four and a half years for continued sexual abuse of two former seminarians, aggravated by his being a minister of religion. Included as a case of a bishop moved to the Vatican, though the victims were adults.
cases.cover_up: After resigning in 2017 amid complaints he was given a post at the Vatican's APSA in December 2017; suspended in January 2019

cases.title: Crimen sollicitationis — secrecy instruction (1962)
cases.who: Holy See — Holy Office (now Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith)
cases.what: The Holy Office instruction Crimen sollicitationis, approved by Pope John XXIII on 16 March 1962 and restating a 1922 instruction, governed canonical cases of solicitation in confession and also obscene acts with pre-adolescent children. It required absolute secrecy under pain of automatic excommunication. Many bishops did not know it was in their archives until press reports in 2003. Canon lawyer Thomas Doyle called the secrecy rules 'an explicit written policy to cover up cases', while others argue it did not bar reporting to police. It stayed in force until 2001.
cases.cover_up: Church proceedings to be kept absolutely confidential under automatic excommunication, binding tribunal members, accusers and witnesses

cases.title: Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela / De delictis gravioribus (2001)
cases.who: Holy See — Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, prefect)
cases.what: Pope John Paul II's motu proprio Sacramentorum sanctitatis tutela (30 April 2001), with the CDF letter De delictis gravioribus of 18 May 2001 signed by its prefect Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, reserved to the CDF the delict of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor under 18, required bishops to notify the CDF after a preliminary investigation, and stated that such cases were subject to the pontifical secret, which remained until December 2019. In May 2014 the Holy See told the UN Committee against Torture that from 2004 to 2013 the CDF had studied 3,420 credible cases of abuse of minors and that 884 priests had been dismissed from the clerical state.
cases.cover_up: All abuse-of-minor cases reserved to the CDF under pontifical secret

cases.title: Pope Francis' letter to Chile's bishops and the Scicluna mission (2018)
cases.who: Pope Francis; Archbishop Charles Scicluna; Mgr Jordi Bertomeu
cases.what: After defending Bishop Juan Barros in January 2018, Pope Francis sent Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, who took 64 depositions in New York and Santiago; their report ran to more than 2,300 pages. In a letter of 8 April 2018 Francis wrote that he had 'made serious errors in the assessment and perception of the situation, in particular through the lack of reliable and balanced information', and summoned the Chilean bishops to Rome, where all of them offered to resign in May 2018.

cases.title: Vos estis lux mundi (2019) and February 2019 summit
cases.who: Pope Francis
cases.what: Three months after a February 2019 Vatican summit of bishops' conference presidents on abuse, Pope Francis issued Vos estis lux mundi, published on 9 May 2019. It requires clerics and religious to report suspected abuse and cover-ups promptly to church authorities, requires every diocese to set up a public reporting system, and lets bishops be investigated for abuse or cover-up. It applies 'without prejudice' to state reporting laws but does not itself require reporting to civil authorities. A revised permanent version was decreed on 25 March 2023 and took effect on 30 April 2023.

cases.title: Pontifical secret lifted for abuse cases (December 2019)
cases.who: Pope Francis
cases.what: On 17 December 2019 Pope Francis issued the instruction 'On the confidentiality of legal proceedings', removing the pontifical secret from cases of sexual abuse of minors and vulnerable persons, child abuse material and concealment of such crimes. Information must still be treated with 'security, integrity and confidentiality' but can be made available to state authorities, and church officials were told to comply with civil laws. In a separate change the same day, the age limit in the Vatican's definition of child abuse material was raised from 14 to 18.

cases.title: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
cases.who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
cases.what: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.
cases.cover_up: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022

cases.title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
cases.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cases.what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.
cases.cover_up: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 100,893 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2005: scandal: Hunan orphanages found buying trafficked babies; 23 officials fired, traffickers jailed 2024: end: China ends intercountry adoption except by blood relatives / stepchildren (5 September)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: China — Uyghur children separated from detained parents and placed in state boarding schools.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. cases.title: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions)
cases.who: Six state orphanages in Hunan; traffickers from Guangdong; local officials
cases.what: Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). cases.title: China — Uyghur children separated from detained parents and placed in state boarding schools
cases.who: Chinese state authorities in Xinjiang
cases.what: As hundreds of thousands of Uyghur and other Muslim adults were detained in Xinjiang, the BBC reported in July 2019, with research by Adrian Zenz, a rapid campaign to build boarding schools and kindergartens with dormitory space, including $1.2bn spent in southern Xinjiang; records showed more than 400 children in one township had lost both parents to internment or prison, and children were assessed for 'centralised care'. School rules imposed points-based punishments on pupils and teachers for speaking anything other than Chinese. Zenz found evidence that children of detainees were being channelled into the boarding system in large numbers. The New York Times reported in December 2019 that about 497,000 pupils were enrolled in such schools. A Xinjiang propaganda official denied that the state was caring for large numbers of parentless children. No sexual-abuse finding is recorded here; this is a child-removal record.

cases.title: Myanmar → China — Kachin women and girls sold as 'brides' (HRW 2019)
cases.who: Traffickers including relatives and acquaintances; buying families in China
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's 112-page report of 21 March 2019 documented women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by conflict, sold for US$3,000–13,000 to Chinese families, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. One survivor was trafficked at 16 by her sister-in-law. The 2025 US TIP report says displaced women and girls in Kachin and Shan remain vulnerable to forced marriage and forced childbearing in China.
cases.cover_up: HRW said Myanmar and Chinese authorities were 'looking away'; police on both sides gave traffickers little reason to fear enforcement.

cases.title: Mongolia — girls sex-trafficked in Ulaanbaatar hotels and karaoke bars (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers in hotels, massage parlours, karaoke clubs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls are sex-trafficked in Mongolian hotels, massage parlours, illegal brothels, bars and karaoke clubs, mostly in Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and border areas, sometimes facilitated by a lack of police enforcement; traffickers use online platforms to groom and blackmail children; and children taken abroad for competitions have instead been put to work, e.g. as horse jockeys.
cases.cover_up: The report says exploitation is sometimes facilitated by lack of police enforcement; some families are complicit.

cases.title: Pakistan → China — 629 girls and women sold as 'brides' (AP 2019)

cases.what: AP obtained a list compiled by Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency of 629 girls and women sold as brides to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. In October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals charged in the biggest case. The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers target impoverished Christian communities to send women and girls to China, where hundreds reported being forced into commercial sex.
cases.cover_up: Officials told AP the investigation largely stopped after June 2019 because of pressure from government officials fearful of harming ties with Beijing; in October 2019 a Faisalabad court acquitted 31 Chinese nationals after witnesses were threatened or bribed into silence.

cases.title: Vietnam and Laos → China — girls sold as brides (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers and marriage brokers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say traffickers in Vietnamese border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriages involving sex trafficking or forced labour, and use 'bride kidnapping' to exploit ethnic-minority girls in the northwest highlands; in Laos, traffickers increasingly kidnap or recruit women and girls via marriage brokers to China for sex trafficking, forced labour and forced surrogacy. Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Iain Wares: Edinburgh → South Africa; Germany → South Africa: Fr Georg Kerkhoff (extradited back).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.role_note: Timothy Omotoso: first report 2017, first action 2017 (0 years). Whistleblower Pamela Mabini was shot dead 7 March 2025, weeks before the verdict; trial delayed eight years by mistrial motions and recusals

Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.

cases.title: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cases.what: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
cases.cover_up: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

cases.title: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse

cases.what: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.

cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Kenya coast — UNICEF/Government study on child sex tourism (2006)
cases.who: Tourists and local clients in Kenya's beach resorts
cases.what: On 19 December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs launched a joint study of four beach resort areas. It found that up to 30 per cent of 12–18-year-old girls living there were involved in casual sex work and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex; 38 per cent of clients were Kenyan and 44 per cent Italian, German or Swiss tourists. Vice President Moody Awori accepted the findings and acknowledged police and community failure to enforce the law.

cases.title: Nyumbani Children's Home, Nairobi — USAID found abuse claims credible
cases.who: Nyumbani Children's Home for HIV-positive children, run by Children Of God Relief Institute (COGRI), a Catholic charity
cases.what: Nyumbani, opened in 1992, was among Africa's first homes for HIV-positive children and attracted large US donations. After a whistleblower complaint, a 2021 USAID investigation found abuse claims 'credible', including rape of children by volunteers, caregivers and other children. The Washington Post reported the findings on 27 November 2023 from court documents filed by the orphanage's Kenyan board. The co-founder stepped down after the Post's questions.
cases.cover_up: A USAID memo (21 July 2022) said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006, 'neglected to document violence against children', permitted victim-blaming and 'systematically failed to respond to widespread sexual misconduct'; some survivors were made to write letters of apology.

flows.what: Cross-border rings ferry women and underage girls from Karamoja to Nairobi for domestic servitude or sex trafficking.

flows.title: Italy / Germany / Switzerland → Kenya coast (tourist offenders)

flows.what: Keith Morris was jailed for 18.5 years in the UK for 10 sexual offences against vulnerable children in Kenya, one of about eight UK prosecutions for offences abroad since 1997.

networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa').
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children from their families were carried out by governments as a matter of policy. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, about 500 babies were taken from mothers held in detention and given to other families; in 2012 a court found this had been a "systematic plan", and by July 2025, 140 of those children had been identified. Under Franco's dictatorship in Spain, children were taken from Republican mothers and later from unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children from their families and placed them in residential schools or with non-Indigenous families. In 1951 Denmark sent a group of Greenlandic children to live with Danish families, and France moved children from the island of Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported children from occupied parts of Ukraine; in March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over these deportations.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Zimbabwe — sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines; girls traded under ngozi (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 238 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Zimbabwe — sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines; girls traded under ngozi (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers at mining sites; families
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and children in sex trafficking around mines, sometimes for money or food, and may exploit children as panners and ore couriers in gold and diamond mines. Traditional practices including trading daughters for food or money and ngozi — giving a relative to another family to atone for a killing — make girls vulnerable. Low-level official complicity persisted.

cases.title: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cases.what: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
cases.cover_up: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

flows.title: UK → Southern Rhodesia child migrants (Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College)
flows.what: IICSA found that children who told the headmaster they had been sexually abused by a padre at the college were beaten and warned against 'spreading malicious lies'; it lacked evidence to say whether Fairbridge UK knew of the allegations.

flows.what: After the 1982 Ruston Report on his beatings was kept from police, Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 and founded Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986. The Makin Review called him 'a problem solved and exported to Africa'.

flows.title: Zimbabwe → South Africa (John Smyth)
flows.what: Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, Smyth moved to South Africa in 2001, attending churches in Durban (from 2002) and Cape Town (Church on Main, 2004–2016). The Makin Review found it highly likely he kept abusing until his death in 2018.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role_note: Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017 (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect networks that abuse children circulate widely. The records gathered for this map show a few cases where a state service was involved, several claims that investigations found to be false, and some that remain unproven. In Chile, Paul Schäfer, who founded the German settlement Colonia Dignidad in 1961, was convicted in 2006 of abusing children there; Chilean officials believe the Pinochet dictatorship used the settlement to torture its opponents, and Germany admitted in 2016 that its embassy had failed to act. In West Berlin, from the late 1960s, the city's youth authorities placed boys in foster care with men known to be paedophiles, on the advice of the psychologist Helmut Kentler. In Afghanistan, US soldiers were told not to intervene when Afghan commanders allied with them abused boys. In Bosnia around 2001, UN police monitors and employees of a US contractor bought women and girls who had been trafficked. In the United States and Australia, police took over websites used to share abuse images and kept them running for weeks or months to identify the users. Investigations found no evidence that MI5 used the Kincora boys' home in Belfast for blackmail, and the ring of powerful men that London police investigated in Operation Midland was invented by Carl Beech, who was later jailed. The claim that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency has not been established.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017
cases.who: Afghan National Defense and Security Forces and Afghan Local Police commanders; US military chain of command
cases.what: In September 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told to ignore sexual abuse of boys by Afghan allies, describing it as rampant; nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) to investigate. SIGAR's report, sent to Congress in 2017 and made public on 23 January 2018, found that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault, and said 'the full extent of child sexual assault committed by Afghan security forces may never be known'. The Pentagon used the 'notwithstanding' exception to the Leahy Law to keep supporting implicated units, including approving continued funding in December 2015 for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.
cases.cover_up: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).

cases.title: Afghanistan — sexual violence against children attributed to the Taliban (UN verified)
cases.who: Taliban de facto authorities
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 12 children (6 boys, 6 girls) in Afghanistan in 2023, 10 attributed to the Taliban, and the abduction of 3 children by the Taliban for sexual violence purposes. It verified 13 cases in 2022 (Taliban 7) and 6 in 2024 (Taliban 5).

cases.title: Afghanistan — students report sexual abuse in Taliban-run madrasahs
cases.who: Taliban-run madrasah system (6,836 male madrasahs per a Feb 2024 UN report)
cases.what: In March 2024 RFE/RL's Radio Azadi published accounts from male students aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs in western and southwestern Afghanistan who said teachers pressured them and classmates into sexual acts and used corporal punishment; some left school. The report cited a February 2024 UN report counting 6,836 Taliban-established madrasahs for boys and a decree seeking 100,000 new madrasah teachers.
cases.cover_up: A 16-year-old said he reported a teacher to the school's qari, who only told the teacher to stop; the teacher admitted it and continued. The schools are run by the de facto Taliban authorities.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: UN peacekeeping data, 2025 (SG report A/80/644): Few finalised: e.g. one Togolese officer — repatriation and 60 days' imprisonment; 'pending additional information from the member state'
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: South Sudan — 'sex for aid' allegations against aid workers, Malakal UN Protection of Civilians site.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.what: A September 2022 investigation by The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022 aid workers in the UN-run Malakal Protection of Civilians site exploited displaced women and girls, including 'sex for aid'; women and girls reported being raped and becoming pregnant. Staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named.

cases.title: Morocco — royal pardon of Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván (2013)
cases.who: Daniel Galván Viña
cases.what: Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, was arrested in Morocco in December 2010 and in September 2011 sentenced to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. In late July 2013 he was among 48 Spanish prisoners pardoned by King Mohammed VI; after protests outside parliament in Rabat, the king revoked the pardon on 4 August 2013, citing the gravity of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. Galván had already left Morocco; he was later arrested in Spain.
cases.cover_up: King Mohammed VI pardoned Galván on 30 July 2013 among 48 Spanish prisoners; he left Morocco on an expired passport with authorities' knowledge before the pardon was cancelled. Protesters in Rabat were violently dispersed. A 2010 US cable reported a 2006 royal pardon of a French man convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh.

cases.title: Morocco — foreign offenders in Tangier vacation rentals (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Foreign nationals, primarily from Europe and the Middle East

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2009: Samoa — Focus on Children (Utah) adoption fraud
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 17,046 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (5% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Luxembourg on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found Middle East and North Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Gulf states block Roblox over child safety (2025)
cases.who: Roblox Corporation
cases.what: In August 2025 Qatar blocked access to Roblox (13 August) and Kuwait's telecoms regulator temporarily blocked it (21 August) after parents and community groups raised child-safety concerns; Turkey had blocked it on 7 August. Roblox had been banned in Oman and Jordan since 2020, and was banned in the UAE from 2018 to 2021. Wikipedia additionally reports that Bahraini MPs drafted a ban, Palestine announced a ban in November 2025, Kazakhstan's and Kyrgyzstan's authorities warned parents about predators, and Buenos Aires and three Argentine provinces blocked it on school devices after grooming reports.

cases.title: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
cases.who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
cases.what: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. Ghana amended its Criminal Code in 1998 to make ritual or customary servitude a crime with a minimum three-year sentence, but the practice continued and no prosecutions are recorded in the source.
